title: Semi-Stalking Yet Another BMW Unicorn

body_markdown:
Those of you who have been reading me for a while know that[I have a thing for BMW wagons](https://bimmerlife.com/2025/09/08/circling-the-wagons-again/) . I owned a 1999 E39 528iT stick sport-package wagon about 15 years ago, which was a very cool car other than eating me alive with its constant needs. I then bought an E46 325XiT stick, which was better reliability-wise, but it was smaller, I didn’t like the way its all-wheel-drive affected the steering feel, and when it needed front CV joints, they were such a pain to replace that I vowed to never own another AWD BMW (for the most part, it doesn’t snow here in Boston *that* often).


My daily driver for the past ten years has been my[2003 E39 530i stick sport](https://www.hagerty.com/media/opinion/the-hack-mechanic/happy-10th-anniversary-you-daily-driver-you/) . With the rear-wheel drive and 5-speed, it’s a wonderfully satisfying car to drive, and with the fold-down rear seats, it has enough cargo space to swallow most of the wheels, tires, Recaro seats, and other automotive accouterments that follow me home. If I need to move anything bigger, I still have the execrable 2008 Nissan Armada. So I don’t *need* a wagon.


Still, my E39 won’t run forever, so I keep my eyes open for a 15-20 year-old E91 BMW 3 Series wagon. On the one hand, I vowed to never own anything newer than an E39/E46 as I don’t want the complexity of not just the all-wheel drive that most later BMWs have, but also the electric water pump, the electrically-assisted steering, and the iDrive controller and the navigation “hump” in the dashboard. However, although nearly all E91 wagons on dealer lots had AWD and automatic transmissions, you *could* order them with rear-wheel drive and a six-speed manual. These are unicorns, and if they also have the sport package (triple unicorn), and don’t have the iDrive and nav hump (quadruple unicorn), they’re enthusiast cars that often pull down twenty grand on Bring a Trailer.


As I wrote about[here](https://www.hagerty.com/media/opinion/the-hack-mechanic/finding-yourself-in-the-automotive-triangle/) , a year ago this spring, a fellow contacted me saying that he had a quintuple unicorn E91 (aluminum interior trim instead of burled wood), knew I wanted one, was preparing to sell his, and offered it to me for eight grand, which was very reasonable for what it was. Unfortunately, he and the car were in Salt Lake City, and I just couldn’t work myself out of[the automotive triangle](https://www.hagerty.com/media/opinion/the-hack-mechanic/finding-yourself-in-the-automotive-triangle/) of price, convenience, and risk. The shipping quote was $1700, flying out there and driving it home wasn’t any cheaper, eight grand turned into ten, and the fact that there was no easy way to see and drive the car before committing to buy it proved to be a bridge too far for a guy who thrives on committing “crimes of opportunity” (buying cars that are close enough to either jump in your daily driver to see and test-drive them, or show up with a truck and a rented U-Haul auto transporter). I offered him seven knowing he’d turn it down, and he did—it sold almost instantly for above his asking price on the E91 forum. I’ve regretted my decision ever since.


But a few weeks ago, a similar E91 wagon showed up on Facebook Marketplace, and this one was just up in New Hampshire and had the eye-poppingly-low price of $5000 “or best reasonable offer.” The description said that it was 6-speed RWD wagon with 145,000 miles that ran and drove well and had a bunch of new parts in it, and that the supplemental restraint light was on due to a bad seat belt tensioner sensor. There were a handful of cell phone pics.


For five grand, this looked promising.


Facebook Marketplace


An interior pic showed a 6-speed knob on the shifter. Unfortunately, the car’s Dakota Terra leather interior looked pretty bad, including large rips in the driver’s seat and trashed-out-looking floors and storage bins. But in the car’s favor, the pic also showed sport seats and steering wheel and no nav hump, raising it to quadruple unicorn status. And, the seller’s location was listed as south-central New Hampshire, just an hour and 45 minutes north of me.


Hello, crime of opportunity? This is Rob Siegel.


This perhaps less so, depending on how you look at it.


Facebook Marketplace


I messaged the seller, professed my intense interest, said that I’d like to come see the car as soon as possible, and that as a semi-retired joe, I could do so at the drop of a hat. While waiting for the reply, I ordered a CarFax (although I didn’t have the VIN, the photos of the car included the license plate). It showed no salvage title, four owners, California and Florida living for the first half of its life, and upstate New York and New Hampshire residence for the second half. It did list a front-end accident in 2022, but it was classified as “minor.” CarFax will also list whatever service records are reported for the VIN in the databases it pulls from, and this showed regular dealer service for the California years, a clutch replacement and other pricey work at a specialty shop in New Hampshire in 2024, then some maintenance at a Meineke there. So far so good.


However, an odd bit on the CarFax was that the current owner appeared to have only owned the car for four months. While people sell cars for all sorts of reasons, this raised the specter that he was bailing out ahead of some expensive repair. It also seemed an odd car for the seller to have, as his Facebook profile indicated he was into off-roading lifted Jeep Cherokees.


Since the VIN was listed on the CarFax, I ran it through a BMW VIN decoder to find out how the car was optioned. Curiously, it didn’t list the transmission type, but it verified that it was a RWD wagon with the suspension, seat, and steering wheel options that comprise the sport package.


Well, okay then!


The seller and I exchanged a couple of messages, I sent him the CarFax and VIN decoder outputs (I believe in buyer and seller having access to the same information), and he said that he could be available after he got off work at 5:30 p.m. I planned to leave after the traffic subsided and shoot for an 8 p.m. arrival.


Then came the question of how aggressively to pounce on the prey. I had undeposited cash from my last car sale, so I was all set there. The hour and 45-minute drive is short enough that I had no issue with simply shooting up there in the 530i to check out the car. If I liked it, bought it, and needed to return again with a second driver or a truck and trailer to get it home, that was fine. But there *is* appeal in knocking it all off in one fell swoop (nothing says “I can make your problem go away” like showing up with cash and a truck and trailer). I found an available auto transporter at a nearby U-Haul. However, it was 90 degrees out, the Armada’s air conditioning had quit working, and I just didn’t have the stomach for a long, hot drive. And, although my back is much better, the idea of having to yank those metal ramps in and out of the trailer concerned me.


As I was about to leave in the 530i, my son Ethan asked me if I wanted him to come along as a second driver so I could bring the car home. I sighed, thought about it, thanked him for his offer, and explained about the quasi-legality of bringing plates from another car and slapping them on (it’s widely done, but at least in Massachusetts, if you’re in an accident, you’re on thin ice if those plates are from a still-registered car). I was fine with keeping it simple and legal and returning another day if I bought it. I loaded the E39 with my plastic ramps (lighter than the floor jack), my Foxwell scan tool, a flashlight, a draft bill of sale, and the envelope of cash, and headed north.


It was dusk when I got to the house. The seller and his young wife and child were in the driveway. We exchanged pleasantries, then I did a walk-around with the flashlight looking at the fender arches, door bottoms, and rocker panels. I saw no rust or even bubbling. I asked the seller if he knew anything about the previous owner’s accident in 2022. “Yeah, he said he hit a snowbank. It cracked the front air dam. You can see it where it’s held together with a zip tie. The left headlight assembly also needed to be replaced, and the left directional still isn’t working.” Certainly not a deal-breaker. And he seemed like an honest young man.


As I walked around the E91, I realized that I hadn’t looked at one in the flesh in years, and was struck by how small it is—it’s a bit under 15 feet long. But that’s not a criticism—the E39 wagon I owned 15 years ago was nearly the size of a Taurus wagon, and it felt a little big to me. This one felt like a trim size.


But looking inside the car put me back on my heels. In addition to the badly-torn driver’s seat cushion, the interior was a mess of energy drink cans, vaping supplies, and clothing. It was even worse than the photos showed. For the life of me I’ll never understand why someone would show a car without taking five minutes to toss this stuff in a bag and put it out of sight. Then again, if it held down the price, great.


I wanted to look under it, so I pulled the ramps out of the trunk of the E39. Unfortunately, it was immediately obvious that the wagon’s sport suspension put it so low that the ramps didn’t come close to clearing the front air dam. However, there was ample clearance for them in the back, so I positioned them there and the owner started the car to back it on. When he did, there was a loud BRAAAAAP from the exhaust that settled into a note that wasn’t deafening but certainly wasn’t quiet. While the engine was still running, I put a gloved hand over the exhaust, and there was no muffling, clearly indicating that it had a leak, and I said so.


“It doesn’t have an exhaust leak,” the owner said (he was incorrect), “but it *does* have the two rear cats removed. The thing was so quiet you practically couldn’t hear it running. I like my vehicles to sound more like *this.* ” He walked over to a rusty old truck that was sitting in the driveway and started it. It was deafeningly loud.


I crawled under the back of the wagon and could see where the two secondary cats had been cut out and pipes had been welded in. I also saw an alarming amount of rust on the rear subframe.


Surprisingly, it was the exhaust that was an immediate issue for me. Here in Massachusetts, at inspection time, if the exhaust sounds at all loud, the inspector does what I did and puts a gloved hand over the tailpipe. If it doesn’t build up exhaust pressure against the hand, the car fails inspection. Further, although the presence of the original catalytic converter configuration isn’t routinely checked, if the car is loud, the inspector can look underneath, and if cats have been deleted, he can fail the car. As I wrote about[here](https://www.hagerty.com/media/opinion/the-hack-mechanic/once-again-we-tackle-the-nissan-armadas-exhaust/) and[here](https://www.hagerty.com/media/opinion/the-hack-mechanic/hack-versus-armada-exhaust-round-iii/) , I went through a ridiculous amount of work getting the Armada through the last three inspections, and it *had* all four of its cats; the problem was in getting the new exhaust to seal against the cats’ rear flanges. The fact that this wagon had an audible exhaust leak *and* was missing both rear cats represented a lot of risk to me—there’s no way it would pass inspection without finding and fixing the leak, and if that couldn’t be set right without setting the whole exhaust right, it could be expensive and time-consuming.


Still, I was interested enough to drive the car. I liked it. It ran and drove fine. Other than the supplemental restraint warning, there were no warning lights on the dash. And even with the leak and the cat delete, the exhaust wasn’t blaringly obnoxious.


Could be worse.


Facebook Marketplace


So, what to do?


I asked the seller why he was selling it after only owning it for just four months. “Actually,” he said, “I’ve had it longer. I got a great deal on it from the previous owner. I’m a mechanic at Meineke. I worked on it for him, then he sold it to me, and I did more work, but it took a while to get the registration transferred.” I remembered the work at Meineke listed on the CarFax. It made sense.


“Still, why sell it?”


He then gave me a surprisingly personal answer: “This house isn’t mine. This is my parents’ house. My wife and kid and I live in a small apartment. I own seven vehicles. I need to make some changes. This one is useless in the snow. I made a snap decision last night to list it and one of the trucks.” I guess that explained why it hadn’t been cleaned. Of course, it also could’ve been that the rusty subframe had a crack in it and he wasn’t telling me.


And so, with that, I asked my signature question: “What do you need to get for it?” I find that, when you ask this (which is a *much* more respectful question than the crass “What’s the lowest you’ll take for it?”), people will often answer it honestly and sometimes even surprise themselves with their own “need to get for it” number. As I’ve said, I don’t negotiate for the sport of it. If I want a car, and the seller names a price I think is reasonable, it’s handshake, money, papers, boom, done. The problem with asking “the question” is that you’re essentially asking them to unilaterally lower their asking price, and if they don’t budge, you’ve kind of cut off your ability to respectfully make an offer. You asked the question. They answered it.


“Well,” he said, “My phone has been blowing up since the ad went up, so what I need to get for it is what’s listed in the ad.” Since the ad said “or best reasonable offer,” I was a bit surprised by this, but even with the car’s issues, his asking price wasn’t unreasonable. I had cash. All I needed to do was extend my hand, say “done,” get a signed title, then come back with a trailer or a second driver.


But instead of doing this, something odd happened. With him firm on the price, I fixated on the exhaust. I painfully remembered buying the Armada knowing that it had an exhaust leak but not where it was or which components needed to be replaced, and it being way more work to deal with than I imagined. I felt like I needed to know what the worst case was in terms of the cost of exhaust components including the cats. I explained all this, and said that even though his car was a well-priced unicorn E91 wagon, I needed to think about it.


“That’s fine,” he said. “I may just pull the ad off Facebook Markeplace. The car probably won’t go anywhere anytime soon. I need to use it this weekend anyway.” We shook hands, and I said that I’d be back in touch.


Should I have bought it on the spot?


Facebook Marketplace


As soon as I began driving off, I thought “OMFG you’re a bloody idiot. You had the E91 RWD stick sport you say that you want sitting in front of you and five grand in your pocket, and you’re walking away from it *over an exhaust issue?? ARE YOU OUT OF YOUR FREAKING MIND???* ” I stopped the car and was about to turn around, but instead messaged him on Facebook Marketplace asking for his cell number in case he took the ad down. He responded immediately. A few seconds later, I got the message from FBM saying the ad had been deleted. I kept driving, thinking that his response and cell number were enough, but also feeling that if I didn’t turn around and buy the car, I’d regret it.


When I got home, I looked up the secondary cats. As I imagined, the dealer price on the full bolt-in pipe was about $1500 list, with a gag-inducing $2,000 core charge (meaning they’re selling rebuilt cats). Not that any sane person would ever pay that. Some used tested cats that needed to be welded in were available on eBay for about $300 a pair. As I’ve said, I don’t weld; I can only bolt exhaust pieces in place. And I’ve yet to find the kind of inexpensive exhaust welding shop that others tell me is ubiquitous in many parts of the country.


There was really no way to know what the car needed until I began working on it. The leak might be unrelated to the cats being cut—a gasket or a metal sealing donut. If I bought it, the strategy would be to seal the exhaust leak and see if the car would get through inspection. If it did, the cats were a moot point. All of this reinforced that I was an idiot to pass on a car I wanted for something as trivial as uncertainty over an exhaust. And really, the whole thing could’ve been avoided if I took another ten minutes, put the car back up on the ramps, crawled back under it, and hunted down the leak.


Regarding the rear subframe rust, reading up on it, it was a more common problem than I was aware of, though I was surprised that it was this bad on a car that lived half its life in California and Florida. Looking on FBM, I *did* see another E91 wagon that someone was bailing out of for $1000 because it needed a rear subframe, but I found numerous videos on YouTube showing replacement. So, concerning, and a lot of work, but not fatal.


So I messaged the seller on his cell saying that I was foolish for passing on the car over an exhaust issue, and that I was sure we could work something out.


When I heard nothing back the following morning, I messaged again, this time being clearer—I said that as long as the air conditioning worked and the vents didn’t smell of rodent (two things I’d forgotten to check), I’d meet his $5000 asking price. I got no response.


I tried one more time—a day later, I found a source on eBay for the seat-bottom cover in the correct Dakota Terra leather for $200, and messaged him saying that the owner might want it, whether that’s him, me, or someone else. Crickets.


I was thrilled to find this, but it didn’t matter.


eBay


I’m not sure if he decided to keep it, if someone offered him more, or if I came across as a Massachusetts suburban dilletante gentleman do-it-yourselfer know-it-all writer and that was too much of a culture clash for a Meineke-working young mechanic living in a small apartment with a young family.


So… did I make a huge mistake or dodge a big bullet?


Initially I felt it was clearly the former, that I let a car I badly wanted slip through my fingers over something trivial, and The Great Automotive Powers That Be would never forgive me for it. But now I’m more of the Larry Bird “I ain’t gonna lose no sleep over it” mindset. Yes, $5000 may be a great price for a unicorn E91 wagon, but you’re paying a premium for both the rarity of the RWD stick sport configuration *and* the rarity of it in a wagon as opposed to the E90 sedan, and really, I don’t need either of them. If the guy contacts me, we’ll take it from there, but I’m not going to show up unbidden at his parents’ house with the trailer and a bag of money trying to make something happen.


At least not yet :^)


***
